dossier.architecture: High-speed swerve, belt elevator, virtual nonparallel four-bar and later cube collector.

subsystems.drivetrain: Custom SDS MK4i top plates add a second drive motor per module: twelve swerve motors total.
subsystems.intake: Roller claw handles cones and cubes; later wide cube collector improves acquisition speed.
subsystems.transfer: Cube collector hands through the wide elevator opening.
subsystems.scoring: Belt-driven elevator and chained virtual four-bar control placement orientation.
subsystems.endgame: No separate lifting mechanism described; team allocated extra motors to drive performance.
subsystems.controls: Three Limelights, dynamic drive-to-node trajectories, 27-button grid selector and piece sensors.

versions: Cube intake added after initial architecture. Sensor-driven automatic stow reduces operator steps after acquisition/release.
dossier.analysis: The strategic package prioritizes reduced travel and alignment time. Distinguish quoted theoretical drivetrain speed from a measured average cycle speed; the latter also includes loading and scoring.
limits: Interview configuration and reported revisions are documented; full season chronology remains to be audited against the linked releases.

context_documents.body:
# 2023-4414: A wide elevator enables a later collector, with a real packaging cost

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A belted elevator and chained virtual four-bar place a shared claw. A later cube collector passes through the elevator opening. The source describes a custom second drive motor on each module and a nominal ratio/speed claim.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly says the wide opening made the late cube handoff possible. Additional drive power is a configuration-specific choice, not a requirement for every copied elevator.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Future expansion space can create strategic flexibility, but extra width and power hardware consume mass and electrical margin from the beginning. Separate the original direct claw from the later cube-assisted acquisition.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure handoff tolerance, frame torsion and loaded drivetrain current before copying the full package.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

## Sources and navigation

- [https://youtu.be/URZEkOANGHQ](https://youtu.be/URZEkOANGHQ)

context_documents.title: Low service burden can require careful construction
context_documents.body:
# 2023-4414: Low service burden can require careful construction

Version: Tsunami interview plus June 29 elevator construction write-up; not one certified event configuration

## Evidence premises

- **team_construction_paraphrase**: Team packages motors inline with the mast base, uses a continuous belt with few redirects and bearing-supported idlers, and adds constant-force return springs. Locator: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-4414-hightide-2023-robot-tsunami/428584?page=8#post_155
- **team_report_not_independent_test**: Team explicitly describes precision-intensive upfront assembly and reports essentially no maintenance after completion. Locator: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-4414-hightide-2023-robot-tsunami/428584?page=8#post_155
- **retained_interview_study**: Existing source study records a shared claw, later wide cube collector, elevator and virtual four-bar, plus automated alignment. Locator: Technical note study6-2023-4414

## Piece flow

Shared-claw path: piece enters the claw and stays with it for placement. Later cube-collector path: cube enters wide collector → crosses an additional transfer through the elevator opening → reaches the scoring claw. Keep those paths distinct; the later robot is not a universal zero-handoff example.

## Physical arrangement and swept space

Elevator rails and moving stages establish the lift corridor; the end-effector linkage occupies additional swept space near the carriage. The through-opening used by the later cube path is a functional packaging feature. Inline base drive placement preserves mast overlap/travel. Belt redirects, tensioning access and return assistance must fit within the same package. Exact battery extraction and collector-to-claw contact geometry remain unresolved.

## Independent motions and powered functions

Lift extension plus end-effector linkage position are distinct functional coordinates; additional acquisition deployment may belong to the later collector. Link count and virtual-link geometry do not establish the number of independent axes. The drivetrain and automation are part of the complete system cost.

## Burdens avoided

Compact rigging can avoid consuming mast travel with bulky base gearing. Careful belt routing can avoid friction that would otherwise demand repeated adjustment. The original shared-claw path avoids a handoff; the later path deliberately spends complexity on acquisition.

## Burdens retained

Belt stiffness, alignment, bearing wear, tension setting, return consistency and precise assembly remain burdens. The team report separates low operating maintenance from manufacturing simplicity. Twelve-motor swerve and advanced alignment controls in the retained source study prevent using Tsunami as proof that every subsystem was minimal.

## Engineering hypothesis

Spend fabrication effort where it produces repeatable motion and reduces event service, while evaluating the full robot on acquisition and scoring. A later wide collector is justified only by a complete-cycle benefit that outweighs its transfer and space costs.

## Rival explanation

The maintenance report may reflect excellent execution, spares or operating conditions rather than a universally forgiving transmission. Fast placement may depend heavily on drivetrain control and driver workflow.

## When the preference reverses

A simpler rigging method may be better if assembly capability, belt quality or alignment control cannot reproduce this construction. A wide collector can be worse if transfer jams dominate the time it saves at acquisition.

## Unknowns

Measured service hours, comparable elevator failure rates, exact collector handoff and verified installation chronology. No CAD release was reviewed. Do not copy nonstandard pulley bend radii from informal feel tests as validated practice.

## Proposed check; not performed

Use a full-stroke clearance and return-force calculation first. If rigging choice remains consequential, test one representative loaded stage path and return consistency, including tolerances and service access; measure complete pickup cycles before adding a collector.

## Outcome evidence

No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.

## Sources

- https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-4414-hightide-2023-robot-tsunami/428584?page=8
- https://youtu.be/URZEkOANGHQ

source_reviews.title: HighTide Tsunami elevator write-up
source_reviews.review_basis: Read team's rigging, bearing, gearbox and tensioning explanation.
source_reviews.facts: Continuous belt drive, inline reduction, supported idlers, belt clamps and return springs.
source_reviews.limitations: Low maintenance is team-reported. No independent endurance data or CAD review.

source_reviews.title: HighTide Tsunami April configuration discussion
source_reviews.review_basis: Read team motor inventory quoted in post 105, virtual four-bar explanation and chassis answer.
source_reviews.facts: One inventory lists 12 swerve motors, powered cube intake, arm rollers and crawler tracks. Unequal sprockets change claw attitude.
source_reviews.limitations: Motor inventory describes a specific configuration. It does not identify match settings or crawler geometry.

source_reviews.title: HighTide Tsunami offseason changes and fabrication discussion
source_reviews.review_basis: Read team updates on Chezy changes, intake impact and roller fabrication.
source_reviews.facts: Chezy arm and wrist replacement, camera tower and ballast. Later posts detail A/B variants and common tube roller construction.
source_reviews.limitations: Descriptions of later intake and roller details do not establish each part's installation at Worlds.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: Tsunami combined a compact swerve base, slanted belt elevator and an arm whose virtual four-bar sets claw pitch as a function of arm angle. The April motor inventory describes separate powered cube intake deployment and rolling, plus a powered arm intake. In that architecture a cone can be carried by the scoring head, while assisted cube pickup requires an additional interface between the collector and head. The exact through-mast path reported in the corpus was not reverified in the written sources. The Chezy configuration replaced the virtual four-bar and head with a different arm-and-wrist design and should be treated separately.
source_review.piece_flow: The arm's head is the placement mechanism. In the April version unequal sprockets change head angle as the arm swings, coupling pickup and placement attitudes to arm position. The separate cube collector provides an alternative acquisition path, with any cube delivered to the arm for elevated placement. The posts establish independent powered functions at both mechanisms. They do not establish the contact order, piece sensor, timing or whether every cube used the collector. For later variants the team documents plastic tube rollers with stretched silicone and printed, glued hubs.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: Drive motors for the elevator are inline with its bottom 2-by-2 tube, preserving travel and overlap. The slant reduces gravity assistance along the guide rails, and the team added four constant-force springs to bring the intermediate stages down. The base is 26 by 26 inches. HighTide reports declining the one-inch module inset it had used on a larger base. Inference: the support footprint, moving mast mass and arm reach jointly constrain acceleration. A wide transfer corridor earns its volume only if the actual collector and arm can intersect safely with a held cube.

subsystems.name: Continuous belt elevator
subsystems.construction: WCP inline blocks with 0.75-inch bearings, 5.6:1 reduction, 36-tooth 18 mm HTD5 drive pulley and fiberglass Gates belt. Printed Onyx redirects are supported through their width. A toothed block and cam tension the belt.
subsystems.operation: Belt runs between the stages. Four constant-force springs help the intermediate stages return through an inclined, low-gravity-assist path.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team wanted compact packaging and more overlap. It selected larger bearings after smaller ones had cracked or worn into tubing.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Return force must overcome worst-case loaded guide and belt friction. Extra bends and belt stiffness consume margin that would otherwise seat stages reliably.
subsystems.interfaces: Base tube carries the gearbox. The moving carriage carries arm loads. Belt clamps and redirects fit within the mast envelope.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check smooth redirects, belt tracking and clamp slip after rebuilds. Compare repeatability on rapid reversals, where sticky stages can settle in the wrong order.
subsystems.unknowns: Belt tension target, stage travel and endurance measurements.

subsystems.name: Arm, wrist and cube intake
subsystems.construction: April arm uses an unequal-sprocket virtual four-bar and powered head rollers. The April inventory gives separate motors for cube roller and deploy. The offseason arm and wrist use lightened 7075 construction.
subsystems.operation: Arm angle determines claw pitch in April. The replacement arm and wrist use roller locations inspired by 1323. Later A/B notes distinguish some intake contact hardware.
subsystems.team_rationale: The offseason changes targeted lower moving mass and improved autonomous reliability. The team reports a roller breaking while the 7075 intake plates survived impacts.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A fixed angular relationship simplifies actuation but constrains the pose family. Measure ground contact and high-node clearance together before changing sprocket sizes.
subsystems.interfaces: The carriage takes the linkage reaction. The collector and claw must share a transfer envelope without fouling the mast or stowed hardware.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Inspect roller cores, glued hubs and pivot lash after contact. Test incomplete transfer and reversal.
subsystems.unknowns: April handoff geometry, linkage ratios and revision-specific pickup sequences.

subsystems.name: Swerve, crawler and vision
subsystems.construction: April inventory lists 12 motors across swerve and one for crawler tracks. Chezy revisions added a vision tower and ballast low behind the elevator.
subsystems.operation: Swerve sets approach position. The tower improves sightlines to retroreflective tape and provides a rear-facing cone-tracking camera for autonomous.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team reports two high autonomous cones became possible without tipping after the changes. It also reports trading practice and readiness for the upgrades.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Extra motors raise demand on packaging and power. Evaluate combined drivetrain and lift load with realistic batteries and loaded acceleration.
subsystems.interfaces: Wheel support polygon and mast loads bound tipping. Camera clearance competes with the slanted elevator and arm.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check approach under voltage sag and verify camera extrinsics after impacts.
subsystems.unknowns: Crawler operation, current limits and quantified vision success.

revisions: April configuration had the virtual four-bar, separate powered cube intake and crawler in the reported motor inventory. At Chezy the team changed the arm/wrist, vision placement and ballast. November posts distinguish A/B intake variants and construction.
transferable_principles: Preserve stage overlap when packaging a lift transmission. Validate force margin for retraction. Treat a mechanically coupled wrist as a designed pose curve.
disconfirming_conditions: Friction or belt bend losses can erase continuous rigging advantages. A cube collector is worthwhile only if broader capture offsets transfer time and failures.
remaining_gaps: Verified April transfer path, crawler function, event installation mapping, exact drivetrain current settings and independent service measurements.

recommended_images.subject: Candidate team illustrations of inline drive, belt redirects and tensioner. Pair with a separate arm pose diagram.
Candidate roller construction image. Label the A/B context.
